Abstract.AI agents for autonomous scientific discovery must decide which experiments to run under a
limited budget. Most benchmarks for science agents provide fixed datasets, while others that support active
experimentation largely rely on simulation. We introduceAutonomous Science Bench, an initial release
comprising six budgeted design–build–test–learn campaigns grounded in published experiments across biology,
chemistry, and materials science. Agents select batches of designs, receive measurements from a lab service,
and use the results to guide subsequent experiments before delivering a predictive model. Success requires
passing two calibrated gates: adiscoverygate, which evaluates the designs the agent measured, and alearning
gate, which evaluates its model’s ranking of held-out designs. In a pilot evaluation of eight agent–model
configurations and 144 trials, the best configuration succeeds in 67% of trials, while the hardest campaign is
solved in only three of 24 attempts. The two gates reveal different weaknesses: some agents build accurate
rankings but find too few promising designs, while others find promising designs but fail to predict which unseen
designs will perform well. These differences are obscured by overall success rates alone. We release version 0.1
of the campaigns, lab runtime, and public leaderboard athttps://yibow.me/autonomous-science-bench.
Correspondence:hanliu@northwestern.edu

4 Results
This section examines how well agents perform and at what cost (Section 4.1), which gate they miss when
they fail (Section 4.2), and how they spend their budget across rounds (Section 4.3). App. B lists the
outcome and both gate scores of every trial.
4.1 Cost and Agent Performance
Overall success is limited.Only 31 of the 144 trials pass. Opus 5.5 in Claude Code resolves 67% of cam-
paign trials, and GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-5.6 Luna in Codex follow at 44% and 28% (Figure 3a). Sonnet 5.5
and GLM-5.3 Flash resolve two trials each, Qwen3.8 27B and MiniMax M3 one each, and Haiku 4.5 none.
Even Opus 5.5 resolves every trial on only two campaigns and fails all three biosensor trials. App. B gives
every configuration’s results by campaign.
Every campaign separates configurations.Each campaign is resolved by some configurations and missed by
others. The oxygen-evolution campaign is resolved most often, in 8 of 24 trials by four configurations, and the
coercivity campaign least, in 3 of 24, two of them by Opus 5.5. Only the two GPT-5.6 configurations resolve
the biosensor campaign. Resolution counts are similar across domains in this sample, at 9, 11, and 11 of 48

6 Limitations
Scale.Version 0.1 contains six campaigns in three fields and evaluates eight agent–model configurations, a small
sample of both experimental science and agents. We plan to add campaigns, fields, and configurations, and a
source registry and contribution guide let research groups contribute campaigns from their own experiments.
Replays and twins.A replay backend returns only previously recorded measurements, while a twin’s reliability
depends on its surrogate’s training coverage. Both limit the design space available to agents.
Public data.The campaigns use published experiments that a model may have memorized or an agent could
retrieve during a trial if egress controls fail to fully block access. Fully addressing them requires unpublished
results from live experiments or autonomous laboratories, which the planned live backend is designed to support.
7 Conclusion
Science advances through decisions about which experiments are worth a limited budget. Autonomous Science
Bench evaluates these choices in campaigns grounded in published lab data, measuring what agents discover and
what they learn separately. Our results show why both matter. Agents can find strong designs without learning
to rank unseen ones, or learn useful rankings without reaching the best designs. Even the strongest evaluated
agent remains unreliable across campaigns, and an overall success rate alone obscures these distinct weaknesses.
We release the campaigns, lab runtime, and public leaderboard as a first step toward evaluation that progress
from replayed experiments through digital twins to autonomous laboratories. As this evaluation moves into
live science, agents will face broader decisions about which questions to pursue and which experiments to run.
The proposed scheduler would allocate scarce measurements to help identify which agents to trust with these
decisions. Together, these steps offer a path toward autonomous science in which agents turn limited experimental
resources into reliable discoveries and new questions worth pursuing.

Jack Foxabbott∗, Arush Tagade, Andrew Cusick, Robbie McCorkell, Leo McKee-Reid, Jugal
Patel, Jamie Rumbelow, Jessica Rumbelow, and Zohreh Shams
Leap Laboratories, London, United Kingdom
June 2025
Abstract
The Discovery Engine is a general purpose automated system for scientific discovery, which com-
bines machine learning with state-of-the-art ML interpretability to enable rapid and robust scientific
insight across diverse datasets. In this paper, we benchmark the Discovery Engine against five recent
peer-reviewed scientific publications applying machine learning across medicine, materials science, so-
cial science, and environmental science. In each case, the Discovery Engine matches or exceeds prior
predictive performance while also generating deeper, more actionable insights through rich interpretabil-
ity artefacts. These results demonstrate its potential as a new standard for automated, interpretable
scientific modelling that enables complex knowledge discovery from data.
1 Introduction
Despite major advances in computational power and data availability, the rate of transformative scientific
discovery has slowed [Bloom et al., 2020, Chu and Evans, 2021, Park et al., 2023]. Much of this stagnation
stems from limitations in the traditional hypothesis-driven scientific method: it is slow, subject to human
cognitive bias, and path-dependent on existing literature. The manual analysis of data remains time-intensive
and vulnerable to oversight, particularly in complex, high-dimensional datasets.
Recent developments in automated machine learning (AutoML) have sought to lower the barrier for
effective modelling by non-experts. However, many existing systems fall short for scientific applications,
in which the objective is to make novel discoveries. They often rely on pre-trained foundation models,
which may come with inductive biases that obscure novel findings. Moreover, while some systems offer
high predictive performance, they often do so at the expense of interpretability, limiting their usefulness in
scientific workflows that demand insight and explanatory power, and preventing their use in safety-critical
domains such as health care and aviation.
To address these challenges, we introduce the Discovery Engine [Rumbelow et al., 2025], a general purpose
automated system for scientific discovery. It combines robust model training with novel interpretability
methods to provide not just

ozone metrics, with
performance typically exceeding 50% for core targets such as daytime average ozone and AOT40. These
results underscore the complexity of tropospheric ozone formation, which involves nonlinear, multi-scale
interactions between emissions, climate, and geography.
Leap’s Discovery Engine outperformed the best baseline model on 14 out of 15 ozone targets. As shown in
Figure 1, its neural networks consistently achieved higher R2 scores than the original baselines, particularly
on high-impact metrics such as the daily maximum 8-hour average ozone ( dma8eu) and vegetation exposure
indices ( AOT40, W90). Importantly, the Discovery Engine also surfaced interpretable, empirically grounded
patterns predictive of ozone extremes. One such pattern, shown in Figure 4, reveals that when the climatic
zone has K¨ oppen climate classification [K¨ oppen, 1936] warm moist or warm dry , and the nitrous oxide
column density falls in the top 10% of observed values, the dma8eu metric is significantly elevated. Existing
literature explains this pattern by enhanced photochemical efficiency under warm conditions, with ozone
production rates increase more rapidly than ozone destruction rates [Meng et al., 2023, Coates et al., 2016].
This kind of multi-factor relationship illustrates the Discovery Engine’s ability not just to improve prediction,
but to support mechanistic understanding and data-driven hypothesis generation in atmospheric science.

4 Conclusion
Our results confirm that the Discovery Engine offers a robust, general-purpose solution to automated scien-
tific modelling. It consistently matches or surpasses benchmarked models from five peer-reviewed scientific
studies, while providing more interpretable results. These interpretability artefacts are not only useful for
explaining model behaviour; they also serve as sources of new empirical insight, revealing patterns that are
non-obvious and often non-linear. Moreover, it does this completely automatically. The papers replicated
here represent weeks or months of work by the original authors, while we completed the analysis in a few
hours. The Discovery Engine has the potential to massively accelerate the research cycle, while reducing
reliance on hypothesis-driven workflows, and mitigating many of the biases that have historically hindered
scientific progress.
By reducing the cognitive and technical burden of data analysis, the Discovery Engine makes exploratory
modelling and data-driven discovery accessible to a wider range of scientists. We believe that this tool
represents a critical step forward in the pursuit of open, interpretable, and efficient science, and sets a
precedent for what automated systems can achieve in advancing human knowledge.

summary: AI agents for autonomous scientific discovery must decide which experiments to run under a limited budget. Most benchmarks for science agents provide fixed datasets, while others that support active experimentation largely rely on simulation. We introduce Autonomous Science Bench, an initial release comprising six budgeted design-build-test-learn campaigns grounded in published experiments across biology, chemistry, and materials science. Agents select batches of designs, receive measurements from a lab service, and use the results to guide subsequent experiments before delivering a predictive model. summary: Detailed profession-specific system prompts raise token use and estimated cost per response without a consistent accuracy gain. We evaluate Scientific Agents, an open-source corpus of 503 profession-specific AGENTS.md profiles, with Gemini 3.8 Flash via OpenRouter in the Pi agent harness. We compare matched profiles with four controls: a minimal baseline ("You are a helpful assistant"), the profile's opening role sentence, a generic scientific rigor guide, and a profile from an unrelated domain. Across nine text-based science benchmarks (4,531 sampled questions, 100 matched profiles), 4,488 items completed all five conditions after API-error retries, scored with automated, rule-based grading. The average profile-baseline accuracy difference is -0.6 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval [-1.5, +0.2] across fixed tasks), and no benchmark shows a statistically clear improvement. Matched profiles produced 1.5-2.3 times as many output tokens and cost 2.2-4.5 times more per successful call. On 60 tool-using BioMysteryBench bioinformatics problems (three runs each for baseline and profile), mean solve rates were 46.7% with the profile and 56.7% at baseline, a difference of -10.0 percentage points (95% interval [-16.7, -3.3]) driven by more frequent token- and time-limit stops under the profile. Longer prompts had one unexpected operational advantage: on SuperGPQA, frequent provider API drops left the short baseline with a correct first-pass answer on only 54.0% of items, against 71.6% with the profile. Generic and mismatched prompts were about as reliable, so this gain comes from prompt length or formatting rather than domain expertise. actions.body: We synthesize recent developments in curiosity-driven learning and computational creativity. Curiosity provides the impetus for exploration in environments with sparse rewards, effectively bootstrapping learning when feedback is deceptive or absent. However, true autonomous research requires moving beyond simple intrinsic motivation. Computational creativity frameworks provide the necessary structure to define, manipulate, and evaluate novel problems. The integration of these components—such as in the CORAL framework—demonstrates the potential for multi-agent evolution to improve upon fixed heuristic searches. Despite these gains, a critical gap persists: current agents operate primarily within bounded, task-specific domains. Future work must bridge the divide between these focused discoveries and the longitudinal scalability required for genuinely open-ended scientific inquiry. Summary: Autonomous agents achieve discovery by balancing intrinsic curiosity with structured problem formulation; however, scaling this capability from specific tasks to persistent, open-ended scientific inquiry remains an unsolved challenge.
actions.lede: How can artificial agents move from task-specific solvers to autonomous investigators?
